title: Text EDA: practice
text:
Generate a few questions about the highlighted conference messages, then choose one to investigate.
Your instructor should first run the completed demonstration and share its data/talk_embeddings.npz file with this project. That file is produced by running the demonstration’s save-vectors cell after local Nomic inference. It is not included in the initial download. Place the instructor-provided file in data/ before starting; then this notebook does not need a running model.
Use the same project folder and .venv notebook kernel. Every row in the CSV retains its official source URL. The 52 short kickers form a selected teaching sample, not a census or random sample.

title: Text EDA: completed demonstration
text:
Question: Which highlighted conference messages express similar ideas, and how do their years and recorded speaker roles relate to those patterns?
We will build one step at a time: a phrase, a kicker, all kickers, a feature matrix, PHATE coordinates, and progressively more informative plots.
Before class, run uv sync, start the Ollama application, and run ollama pull nomic-embed-text:v1.5. Open this project folder in Positron and choose its .venv notebook kernel. All file paths below are relative to that folder.
The embedding calls use your local Nomic model. Model results will appear when you run the notebook.
Teaching route: Sections 1–18 build the main demonstration. Section 19 is an optional refit extension. Finish with the discussion, then use the save-vectors and Plotly publishing sections as needed.
Run cells from top to bottom. In the live scaffold, complete each TODO before running the cells that use its result. To prepare student practice, run the save-vectors cell once and share data/talk_embeddings.npz with the project.

title: Text EDA: completed demonstration
section: 1. Embed one simple phraseNomic uses task prefixes. clustering: asks for representations useful for grouping texts by common content. It does not run a clustering algorithm. We will use the same prefix throughout.
text:
1. Embed one simple phraseNomic uses task prefixes. clustering: asks for representations useful for grouping texts by common content. It does not run a clustering algorithm. We will use the same prefix throughout.

import ollamaMODEL = "nomic-embed-text:v1.5"phrase = "Helping a neighbor through a difficult time."phrase_response = ollama.embed(    model=MODEL,    input="clustering: " + phrase,    truncate=False,)

3. Predict, then repeat the same callWhich two phrases should be most similar? What might happen with the negated sentence? Predict before running. The model supplies a learned representation; it may not handle every comparison as you expect.

phrases = [    "Helping a neighbor through a difficult time.",    "Offering support to someone facing hardship.",    "The train arrives at the station at noon.",    "Refusing to help a neighbor through a difficult time.",]phrase_vectors = []for text in phrases:    response = ollama.embed(        model=MODEL,        input="clustering: " + text,        truncate=False,    )    phrase_vectors.append(response["embeddings"][0])

No model or dimensionality reduction method is refitted.To inspect one speaker instead, change the condition to, for example, keep = df["speaker"] == "Russell M. Nelson", then rerun the filtering and plotting cells. This displays only five talks in this sample, so use the larger year subset for the optional refit demonstration.
text:
18. Filter the displayed talksSuppose we want to inspect 2023 and later. Selecting rows keeps their existing PHATE coordinates. No model or dimensionality reduction method is refitted.To inspect one speaker instead, change the condition to, for example, keep = df["speaker"] == "Russell M. Nelson", then rerun the filtering and plotting cells. This displays only five talks in this sample, so use the larger year subset for the optional refit demonstration.

keep = df["year"] >= 2023recent = df.loc[keep].copy()print("Displayed talks:", len(recent), "of", len(df))recent[["title", "year", "PHATE1", "PHATE2"]].head()

Keep the original axis ranges and year scale so the filtered view uses the same visual reference frame. Otherwise automatic rescaling could make the same coordinates or years look different.

fig = px.scatter(    recent, x="PHATE1", y="PHATE2", color="year",    hover_name="title", hover_data=["speaker", "kicker"],    range_x=[df["PHATE1"].min(), df["PHATE1"].max()],    range_y=[df["PHATE2"].min(), df["PHATE2"].max()],    range_color=[df["year"].min(), df["year"].max()],)fig.show()

Investigate: Choose a question about the year or role comparisons. Read at least three kickers, identify a complication, and state one next check. The selected sample cannot establish historical trends across all talks.## 19. Extension: subset the vectors and refitFiltering asks where selected talks lie in the original map. Refitting asks for a new view of variation within that subset. These answer different questions. Start with a sufficiently large subset, such as our 2023-and-later records, rather than only two or three talks.

recent_vectors = X[keep.to_numpy()]recent_coordinates = phate.PHATE(random_state=386).fit_transform(recent_vectors)recent["PHATE1_refit"] = recent_coordinates[:, 0]recent["PHATE2_refit"] = recent_coordinates[:, 1]fig = px.scatter(    recent, x="PHATE1_refit", y="PHATE2_refit", color="year",    hover_name="title", hover_data=["speaker", "kicker"],    range_color=[df["year"].min(), df["year"].max()],)fig.show()

Discuss: Which relationships seem to persist? The refitted map may rotate, reflect, rescale, and change shape. Its coordinates are not directly comparable with coordinates from the full fit. Check the actual texts and their original vectors rather than interpreting movement across maps as change in the talks.## Finish the discussion here- What question did the next plot help you answer?- Which kickers support your explanation, and which complicate it?- What did filtering do? What changed when we refitted?- What can the short kicker and selected sample leave out?State one finding using this pattern: **In this selected sample, we noticed ; the kickers  support this, while ___ complicates it. Our next check would be ___.** There is no need to return to the slides.## Optional: save the real vectors for laterAfter completing the demonstration, save a single file. Keep row identifiers and texts with the vectors so a later notebook can check their alignment. This is introduced after the visible embedding loop, not hidden inside it. The practice notebook can then work without a running Ollama model.

np.savez_compressed(    "data/talk_embeddings.npz",    embeddings=X,    talk_id=df["talk_id"].to_numpy(dtype=str),    kicker=df["kicker"].to_numpy(dtype=str),    model=np.array(MODEL),    prefix=np.array("clustering: "),)

To reuse those vectors in a later session after loading the same CSV:pythonsaved = np.load("data/talk_embeddings.npz", allow_pickle=False)assert saved["model"].item() == MODELassert saved["prefix"].item() == "clustering: "assert np.array_equal(saved["talk_id"], df["talk_id"].to_numpy(dtype=str))assert np.array_equal(saved["kicker"], df["kicker"].to_numpy(dtype=str))X = saved["embeddings"]A different model, changed text, or a changed row order requires a matching set of vectors.
## 20. Publish a Plotly figure inside a Quarto pageExport the full-data figure constructed before filtering. Its JavaScript is included, so it can be opened independently of Python or hosted on GitHub Pages. This figure supports hover, pan, zoom, and legend interaction; filtering remains ordinary pandas code in the notebook.

full_map.write_html("talk_map.html", include_plotlyjs=True)


Embed the exported figure in your .qmd1. Run the export cell above. Keep talk_map.html next to index.qmd at the project root, rather than putting the only copy inside docs/.2. Paste the following into index.qmd (or another .qmd in the same folder):`markdown````3. This project already has the following entry under `project.resources` in `_quarto.yml`:yamlproject: resources: - talk_map*.htmlFor a different project, merge that resource entry into its existing `project` configuration. Do not replace the rest of its configuration. Quarto copies the exported HTML into the rendered website so the relative iframe URL also works on GitHub Pages.4. Save the files, then run from the project terminal:bashquarto preview``No Ollama request is made by previewing the page: the figure is already exported. After editing the plot, rerun its export cell and preview again. To publish, runquarto render, commit the updateddocs/, and use the repository's/docsGitHub Pages source.The homepage also includes a tiny three-point publishing example that works immediately without model inference. Once your real talk map exists, use the same iframe pattern withtalk_map.html`.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Why do we do EDA?
text:
Why do we do EDA?
We explore data to understand what it contains, investigate questions, and discover what to examine next.
Think of the Titanic or tornado investigation:
What did a useful new plot help you notice or ask?

0:00-1:30 including title. Take one or two short contributions. Examples: compare proportions rather than counts, reveal a relationship, identify an unusual observation, or check an explanation. Emphasize that a question guides the next operation and the result can change the question. This is a bridge from the earlier work, not an isolated quiz about embedding interpretation.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Why did dimensionality reduction help?
text:
Why did dimensionality reduction help?
One observation can have many numerical features.
Dimensionality reduction gives us a small number of coordinates for a view of those observations.
Color and the original data help us interpret the view.
What information might a two-dimensional view leave out?

1:30-2:30. Recall how a passenger’s many prepared features became two plotted coordinates. A map compresses information, so we still investigate original observations. Keep this review conceptual; the focus today is applying the familiar workflow to text. Students should recognize the familiar role of a feature matrix.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: What if an observation is a piece of text?
text:
What if an observation is a piece of text?
“Helping a neighbor through a difficult time.”
We can read the words, but what numbers should describe the observation?
We want to investigate which messages express related ideas, even when their wording differs.

2:30-3:30. Ask for one idea, such as word counts or word indicators, but do not start another text-processing lesson. Motivate a learned representation as one option. The same EDA question now needs a different way to construct features.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: A model turns text into a vector
text:
A model turns text into a vector

Two phrases pass through the same text encoder and become fixed-length vectors. Numerical entries are illustrative.Related texts can have similar vectors. Individual coordinates usually do not have convenient topic names.

Simplified redraw of Reimers & Gurevych (2019), Sentence-BERT, Fig. 2: paper, CC BY-SA 4.0. Architecture details omitted; this is not Nomic’s exact architecture.


3:30-5:00. One input string becomes one fixed-length vector. The model has been trained previously; we are applying it rather than training it in class. The two uses of the encoder share the same trained model. The illustrative numbers help show the type and shape of the output, not an actual model result. Explain that an embedding is a representation, not a generated prose answer and not a list of named topics. The redraw removes SBERT-specific architecture details and the similarity-computation node to focus on text-to-vector conversion.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Predict before computing
text:
Predict before computing

Helping a neighbor through a difficult time.
Offering support to someone facing hardship.
The train arrives at the station at noon.
Refusing to help a neighbor through a difficult time.

Which pair should be most similar? Which comparison might challenge the model?

5:00-6:30. Give students a short partner discussion. Sentences 1 and 2 express related ideas with different words; sentence 4 tests negation despite shared wording. Do not promise a particular model score or ranking. The notebook later computes actual Nomic results so we can compare the prediction with the evidence.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Comparing two vectors
text:
Comparing two vectors
Cosine similarity compares their directions:
\[
\operatorname{cosine}(u,v)=\frac{u^\top v}{\|u\|_2\|v\|_2}
\]
Same direction: 1. Perpendicular: 0. Opposite directions: -1.
The score is a comparison under this representation, not a probability of identical meaning.

6:30-7:30. The formula requires nonzero vectors. Connect the dot product and vector norm to linear algebra. We will use a familiar two-coordinate example before considering hundreds of coordinates. A high score cannot by itself establish that two statements make the same claim, especially with negation.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: A two-dimensional example
text:
A two-dimensional example

Arrows u=(1,0), v=(1,1), and w=(0,1) show an angle of 45 degrees between u and v.\[
\operatorname{cosine}((1,0),(1,1))=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\approx0.707
\]
What is the similarity between u and w?

7:30-9:30. Work the numerator 11+01=1 and lengths 1 and sqrt(2). The second answer is 0. Ask what would happen for (-1,0), giving -1. These are deliberately simple geometric vectors, not a projection of Nomic features. The completed notebook includes the same calculation with NumPy, so students can inspect every operation.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Where does the model run?
text:
Where does the model run?

A cloud request reaches a provider’s model, while a local request reaches Ollama and a downloaded model on the same computer.Cloud services supply the computing hardware. Local use requires a downloaded model and suitable hardware on your computer.

9:30-11:00. Students have mostly encountered cloud models. Both approaches can be called from Python. In this lesson a cloud request crosses the computer boundary; the local request goes to a service on the same computer. Avoid claiming that all cloud systems or all local systems have identical privacy/performance properties. After the initial download, this lesson’s local inference uses the downloaded model. Ollama also has cloud features; we are demonstrating its local path. Source: https://docs.ollama.com/faq.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Ollama runs the model for us
text:
Ollama runs the model for us

Ollama application: downloads and runs models.
Nomic model: supplies the learned text-to-vector transformation.
Python package: lets our notebook request embeddings.

Install the application, start it, and download the model before class. Installing the Python package alone does not start the application.

11:00-12:00. Connect the local service to the earlier client/server and API material. The notebook is the client. The Ollama application serves requests, normally on localhost:11434. No cloud API key is needed for this downloaded model. Students should distinguish the serving tool from the trained model and its Python interface. Source: Ollama documentation.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Our model: nomic-embed-text:v1.5
text:
Our model: nomic-embed-text:v1.5
A pretrained text embedding model available through Ollama.

Returns a numerical vector rather than a chat response.
Normally produces 768 values per input; inspect the actual result.
Uses a task prefix. We will consistently use clustering: for grouping similar messages.


Nomic model card · Ollama model


12:00-13:00. The prefix is part of the input convention documented by Nomic; it does not perform a clustering analysis. Use the same model and prefix for phrases and kickers. Distinguish model embedding dimensions from the later two-dimensional visualization. Avoid a long model benchmark comparison or architecture discussion.

title: From Text to Exploratory Plots
section: Ask for an embedding
text:
Ask for an embedding
import ollama

response = ollama.embed(
    model="nomic-embed-text:v1.5",
    input="clustering: Helping a neighbor.",
    truncate=False,
)
vector = response["embeddings"][0]
We will inspect the response, the vector length, and a few values before doing anything more complicated.

13:00-14:00. The endpoint can return several embeddings, so a single input still gives an outer list; [0] selects its first vector. truncate=False makes overlong inputs an explicit error. Do not unpack a complicated helper function or introduce batch caching here. The next step in the notebook repeats the same visible call for a few phrases. Source: https://docs.ollama.com/api/embed.

A phrase → one kicker → all kickers → a feature matrix → PHATE → plots that help answer a question.

Use the question about similar highlighted messages and their years/recorded roles to motivate each added plotting argument.
